items.title: The Night the Count Stood Still
items.content_html:
The Night File — The Desk’s Report

Objective

The Night the Count Stood Still

At 0400 no new race had been called in the night. What the night produced instead was the calendar: the dates on which Mississippi and Alaska will finish, stated plainly; a narrower margin in Colorado’s 4th; a second Asian selling of the chip trade; oil testing $93; a draft agreement circulating in Doha with no signature on it; and the vice president’s full accounting of the defeat, printed where his party could read it.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0400 ET, Thursday, November 5, 2026. This edition continues the log of the midterm count from Edition No. 5, the Midnight Watch. Where the overnight reporting corrects a procedure this paper carried on Wednesday—Mississippi’s, below—the correction is printed in the open and the earlier editions stand unrevised, as a log stands.

The Night in Brief

No call moved in the night, in either chamber, in any state. The Senate stands where the midnight edition left it: 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with Alaska and Mississippi uncalled. The Associated Press House tracker in its latest state is also unchanged: 235 seats won by Democrats and 26 led, against 146 won and 28 led for Republicans, with 26 seats still too close to call. The governorships stand at 28 for the Democrats with Alaska and Kansas open. Control of no chamber and no majority is in question in any count on the shelf. The night’s work was not the result; it was the schedule on which the remainder of the result will arrive, and the readings that Asia, Tehran, and the Republican Party’s own vice president put on the result while Washington slept.

Two facts organize the night: the remaining counting is now dated—Mississippi certifies by November 13, Alaska tabulates on November 18—and the war is still unsettled, with a draft circulating in Doha, unverified claims of fresh tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, and oil priced as if the war were ending anyway.

Mississippi: The Calendar, Stated Plainly

The overnight explainer, carrying the Associated Press’s account, corrects the procedure this paper printed on Wednesday, and the correction is filed first. Mississippi does not require a majority in a regular federal general election. The candidate with the most votes wins; there is no runoff. The December 1 runoff date carried in Editions No. 2, 4, and 5 of this paper does not apply to this race, and the desk withdraws it here, in the next edition in the log, which is where a log corrects itself. The count itself stands as the midnight edition left it in its latest figure: the Democrat, Scott Colom, at 464,926 votes, 49 percent, and the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, at 463,788, 48.9 percent—a margin of 1,138 votes, with an estimated 96 percent of votes counted, per the account of why the two Senate races have not been called filed below. Al Jazeera’s account of the same delay carries the same margin and the same leader.

What remains, and by when: approximately 3,600 absentee-by-mail ballots still to be received within five business days, and an unknown number of affidavit ballots, per the November 4 statement of Michael Watson, the secretary of state, quoted in both accounts. A voter who cast an affidavit ballot for lack of acceptable identification has until November 10 to present it. Counties have until November 13 to submit certified results. Mississippi holds no automatic recounts; a candidate seeking one would have to obtain a court order, per the Associated Press. The wire calls a race when the trailing candidate has no path left to close the gap; here the path runs through several thousand ballots against a margin of 1,138, and it stays open until they are counted.

Alaska: Eleven Days of Mail, Then the Tabulation

Alaska’s Senate count did not move in the night; its procedure is also now fully stated. The Associated Press Senate file still shows 75.43 percent of precincts reporting, and the Democrat, Mary Peltola, still leads the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan—by 626 votes in the Associated Press figures carried in the overnight explainer, and by 637 in the same wire’s evening dashboard entry carried in the midnight edition. The desk prints both numbers; they are two states of one unfinished count. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holds 3,583 votes, more than either margin. Alaska accepts domestic mail ballots for up to 10 days after Election Day and overseas ballots for up to 15 days, provided they were mailed by November 3. If no candidate clears 50 percent of first choices—both leaders are below it—the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18.

The legal file around the count, stated without weight on either side: the Justice Department sued to block certification if the incumbent loses; Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit on November 1, ruling that the government had offered no workable plan to investigate ballots cast for the second Sullivan while preserving ballot secrecy; the department has said it will appeal. The governor, Mike Dunleavy, has ordered a state investigation and has suggested he may not certify a Peltola victory, per the Associated Press account filed below. Peltola has said her campaign had no involvement in the second Sullivan’s candidacy, and he has said he had no contact with her campaign about running. Each statement stands as its maker made it. In the governorship, the Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, holds 49.2 percent of first choices with about 74 percent counted, the Republican Bernadette Wilson second at about 29 percent—the same November 18 schedule if no majority emerges.

Colorado and Kansas: The Counts That Moved

Colorado’s 4th District narrowed in the night, toward the incumbent. The Associated Press count in its latest state shows the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 176,162 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 173,649—a margin of 2,513 votes, with 92.64 percent of precincts reporting. The midnight edition carried the same file at 174,963 to 171,711, a margin of 3,252. The race remains too early to call. The account of the incumbent’s path filed below puts about 30,000 ballots outstanding, concentrated in Douglas and Larimer counties, and records her own figure from Wednesday evening: “We’re about a 5,000-vote deficit right now, a little bit less than that.” Colorado’s deadline for military and overseas ballots to arrive, and for voters to cure a missing or mismatched signature, is November 12.

Colorado’s 3rd District is reported two ways, and the desk prints both. The midnight edition, following the Colorado live file as it signed off for the night, carried the Democrat, Dwayne Romero, leading the Republican incumbent, Jeff Hurd, by more than 2,200 votes with 88 percent counted. The Rocky Mountain Voice file, in an update timed 8:22 a.m. Wednesday, reports Hurd ahead by 1,211 votes. The two files cannot both describe the same state of the count; they were taken at different hours from different tallies, and the race is uncalled in both. Which man leads the 3rd District at 0400 is a question the next counts will answer, and it is filed here as open.

Kansas’s governorship did not move in the night, and its audit is now general. The Associated Press Kansas file stands at 549,974 votes for the Democrat, Cindy Holscher, and 542,929 for the Republican, Ty Masterson—a margin of 7,045, with all precincts reporting, the race still too early to call. The secretary of state, Scott Schwab, has ordered close-race audits in six races that finished within one percent—governor, secretary of state, attorney general, and three state House districts—each a hand count of ballots in 10 percent of precincts, per the account of the audits filed below. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day and received by Friday will be added. Holscher has declared victory; Masterson has not conceded; the governor, Laura Kelly, has congratulated Holscher as governor-elect. All three statements stand, and the count proceeds underneath them.

Asia: The Second Selling of the AI Trade

Asia’s Thursday session repeated Wednesday’s pattern in sharper form: the chip trade sold, and nearly everything else rose. Reuters’ Singapore file reports oil, chip stocks, and the dollar under pressure and broad indexes higher, on the same reasoning the American session used: a clear electoral outcome, and the expectation—an expectation, not an agreement—that the war with Iran will end sooner under a Democratic Congress. Brent crude futures fell nearly 9 percent overnight, below $100 a barrel, and stand about 20 percent lower on the week; if the fall holds through Friday’s close it is the largest weekly drop since April 2020, when American crude briefly traded below zero. In the Asia morning Brent was testing its lows at $93.50; a Dow Jones account carried front-month Brent at $93.85, down 0.8 percent on the day in Asia, and West Texas Intermediate at $86.93, down 1.4 percent. The dollar fell to a one-month low of $1.1273 per euro. The ten-year Treasury yield fell 6 basis points overnight and a further point in early Tokyo trade, to 4.87 percent.

The selling sat in the same names, and the percentages differ by the hour each file was taken. Reuters’ morning figures: the KOSPI down 4 percent and near a seven-month low, Taiwan down 1.8 percent, the Nikkei down 0.5 percent. The Asia-Pacific market file filed below, taken later in the session, carries the KOSPI down about 4.8 percent after a sidecar—a five-minute halt to program trading—was triggered, the Nikkei down about 1.5 percent while the broader Topix rose about 1.4 percent, Shanghai up about 3.6 percent, and the Hang Seng up about 3 percent. SoftBank fell about 5.8 percent, on the slide in its chip designer Arm and a Financial Times report that Chinese regulators will not allow its $5.4 billion acquisition of ABB’s robotics division. Solar shares rose the most in the Reuters account; data-centre companies and their suppliers fell across Asia. In India, the Nifty 50 rose more than 2 percent to 24,442.20 and the Sensex more than 2 percent to 79,001.19, on the fall in crude. Gold extended Wednesday’s rise of about 3 percent to about $4,135 an ounce. A Melbourne strategist quoted by Reuters states the markets’ position in one sentence: “The magnitude of the victory is what has caught markets off guard.”

The Strait and the Draft

No agreement was announced in the night, and the two public accounts of the talks do not describe the same distance. On one bearing, a draft is close: reports carried in the Indian market coverage state that the United States has approved a draft understanding passed to Iran through Qatari mediators, and the account of the Qatar-presented draft filed below reports that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were briefed and approved it, that concessions cover Iran’s nuclear program and its frozen assets, and that the timing of simultaneous announcements is under discussion. On the other bearing, the distance stands: a senior Iranian official told Reuters the two sides remain far from a deal, that Tehran’s conditions must be met if the United States wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened, and that feedback on the mediators’ latest suggestion was expected from both capitals within 36 hours; the Qatari team has returned to Doha and the talks continue through the mediators, per the Reuters account of the diplomatic push filed below. Iran’s stated basis remains its seven-step plan of September: an end to the American naval blockade, a waiver on oil sales and cancellation of new sanctions, reopening of the strait—which Tehran says it can now do within two days of an agreement—and talks on the remaining issues, including the nuclear program, to follow. The secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, has said the American reply was not convincing and all seven conditions must be answered clearly. From Washington there is no agreement and one sentence of posture: the president has said the United States has no immediate plans for military action.

Two further facts stand beside the talks, each attributed. First, Tehran is on high alert: two senior Iranian sources told Reuters that while Iranian leaders welcomed the Democrats’ victory, they were concerned the president could seek to compensate for it with a military strike, per Reuters’ account of the Iranian response filed below. Second, the strait itself produced claims in the night that the desk cannot verify and prints as claims: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in the strait and that a tanker using an unapproved route had struck a mine, per the Asia-Pacific market file; a separate report carried the Guards’ navy saying three oil tankers hit mines on Tuesday. No second source on the shelf confirms either incident. Oil fell through both claims, which is a fact about the market’s reading, not about the strait.

The Vice President’s Accounting

The fullest Republican document of the night is the vice president’s, and it was published where his own party reads. Le Monde’s overnight analysis carries the post in substance. JD Vance wrote: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.” And: “To the people who are pissed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so.” The post’s analysis of the vote is that the loss was not a turnout failure: many people who voted for the Trump–Vance ticket in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. Its four lessons are ending the war in Iran, focusing on the cost of living, adhering to the America First doctrine, and reassessing the relationship with Israel. On immigration enforcement, the vice president wrote that he is open to changing the approach, for instance by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor.

The rest of the party’s argument ran in the same hours, in the open. The president, asked at the White House ballroom construction site about the vice president’s assessment, answered: “Well, I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term, and probably that’s true, but at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because, long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, who leaves office in January, described the midterms as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans.” The commentator Rod Dreher, long close to the vice president, wrote that the president should resign and let the vice president run things for the next two years, and called him a spent force; the commentator Matt Walsh called him, on Tuesday evening, “yesterday’s news.” The Speaker, Mike Johnson, announced Wednesday morning he will not seek the leadership of the Republican minority in January. Former Ambassador Nikki Haley stated the contrary lesson: “When we stay close to our policies, we win: economic freedom, lower taxes, smaller government, making sure we get families back to work, national security.” Nothing in the argument was settled overnight; the 2028 succession is now an open question inside a party that still holds the White House, the veto, and the command of the armed forces.

The World’s Morning Papers

Europe’s second-day readings divide between welcome, caution, and the judgment that nothing structural has changed. The roundup of the world leaders’ reactions filed below carries them in sequence. Germany’s defense minister, Boris Pistorius, congratulated the Democrats on a historic victory and stated that Europe must continue assuming greater responsibility for its own security. France’s economy and finance minister, Roland Lescure, called the gains undeniable and cautioned that the president retains significant authority over American foreign policy. Italy’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, said the results would not alter relations between Rome and Washington. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, welcomed the victory as a positive development for American democracy; the Czech prime minister, Andrej Babiš, called it expected but exceptionally large. The co-leader of Germany’s AfD, Alice Weidel, stated the reading from the other side of her country’s politics: the president had promised his voters no interventionist foreign policy, and the broken promise had come back to haunt the Republicans. Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, stated the cost-of-living reading in general form: “The world now has an opportunity to unite around an issue that affects us all, and that’s the cost of living.” Belgium’s defense minister, Theo Franken, stated the governing reading: with so many internal divisions, it will be nearly impossible to govern in the United States over the next few years.

The other capitals held the positions the earlier watches recorded. China’s foreign ministry spokeswoman, Mao Ning, described the election as a domestic matter that will not change Beijing’s position. The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, expressed hope that the president would continue pursuing diplomatic solutions; the deputy foreign minister, Sergei Ryabkov, counseled waiting for the final results. In Tehran, the newspaper Hamshahri printed the anniversary of the 1979 embassy seizure beside the election under the headline “Iran’s shadow over US elections,” with an image of the president blindfolded and his head bowed. In London, the Guardian’s readers divided between enthusiasm and the repeated caution that Washington may return to business as usual. Each capital’s reading is printed as that capital made it; the disagreement is itself the record of the night abroad.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Colorado’s 3rd District: one Colorado file carries the Democrat ahead by more than 2,200 votes as its night closed, another carries the Republican ahead by 1,211 in a Wednesday-morning update—the leader itself in dispute until the next counts. Second, the Asian percentages: the KOSPI down 4 percent in the morning file and about 4.8 percent in the later one, the Nikkei down 0.5 and about 1.5, Brent at $93.50, $93.85, and about $97 in three files taken at different hours of one falling market—a disagreement of clocks, printed because a reader checking any one file against this page will find the other numbers. Third, the talks in Doha: one set of reports has a draft approved in Washington and welcomed in two Gulf capitals, and the named Iranian officials on the record say the American reply is unconvincing and the two sides far apart. Both bearings are printed above; an agreement exists when both capitals announce one, and neither has. Against the triangle, the load-bearing facts of the night are single-valued: no race was called; Mississippi’s calendar runs to November 10 and 13 with no runoff in the procedure; Alaska’s runs to November 18; Colorado’s 4th narrowed to 2,513 votes; oil fell below $100 and tested $93; and the vice president’s sentence—“The reason we lost is the war”—stands unretracted, with the president’s answer beside it. The log proceeds on the clerks’ schedules now, not on Washington’s. The next count belongs to the states.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-four items.

Subjective
The Business Standard — why Alaska and Mississippi have not been called

The Associated Press had not called either Senate race by Thursday. Mississippi: Colom leads Hyde-Smith by 1,138 votes, about 3,600 mail ballots outstanding, affidavit identification due by November 10, counties to certify by November 13, the most votes wins with no runoff, and no automatic recount. Alaska: Peltola leads Sullivan by 626 votes, mail accepted for 10 days domestic and 15 overseas, ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18, the certification suit dismissed November 1 with an appeal stated, and the governor’s race on the same schedule.

Subjective
Al Jazeera — what is delaying the two Senate calls

Colom ahead by 1,138 votes on Wednesday night with about 96 percent counted and a few thousand provisional and mail ballots left; Peltola ahead by 637 with nearly a quarter of Alaska’s votes uncounted; Mississippi’s 10 days to process and five business days for mail; Alaska’s ranked-choice results to be published November 18.

Subjective
Agence France-Presse, via Ekkow — Mississippi cliffhanger, Alaska count continues

The two uncalled Senate races on Wednesday: Colom ahead by less than 50 votes in the CNN and NBC counts the story cites, with thousands of eligibility-check ballots uncounted; Peltola at 48.2 percent to Sullivan’s 47.9 with 74 percent counted; the second Sullivan at 3,583 votes, more than the 626 separating the front-runners; and a result that may not be declared for weeks.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 35 races listed, Alaska too early to call at 75.43 percent of precincts reporting, Mississippi too early to call at 99.83 percent, and the remaining races called state by state.

Subjective
Associated Press — House balance of power

235 House seats won by Democrats and 26 more led, against 146 won and 28 led for Republicans, in the tracker’s latest state—unchanged overnight.

Subjective
Associated Press — Colorado’s 4th District

Laubacher 176,162, Boebert 173,649, with 92.64 percent of precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Times Now World — Boebert trails in Colorado

The incumbent’s path described as increasingly difficult, with about 30,000 ballots outstanding in Douglas and Larimer counties, the shares she would need in each to close the gap, and her Wednesday-evening statement: “We’re about a 5,000-vote deficit right now, a little bit less than that.”

Subjective
Rocky Mountain Voice — Colorado’s federal races

The state file with its Wednesday update: Hurd pulled ahead of Romero in the 3rd District by 1,211 votes as of 8:22 a.m.; the 3rd, 4th, and 5th districts uncalled; the 8th settled for the Democrats; Douglas County’s count in the 4th, where Laubacher leads with half the district’s registration; and November 12 as the deadline for overseas ballots and signature cures.

Subjective
Associated Press — Governor, Kansas

Holscher 549,974, Masterson 542,929, with all precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Johnson County Post — Kansas orders audits in six close races

Six races within one percent to be audited by hand count in 10 percent of precincts: governor, secretary of state, attorney general, and House Districts 27, 40, and 117. Holscher’s victory statement, Masterson’s answer that the margin calls for another look, and the sitting governor’s congratulations to the governor-elect are printed in the same story.

Subjective
State Capital Lobbyist — where things stand, Wednesday evening

The standing accounting the night began from: the Senate at 54 to 44 with two uncalled, 26 House seats open, 28 governorships held by the Democrats, and at least nine legislative chambers flipped, every one in the same direction.

Subjective
Reuters — oil and data centre stocks sink in Asia

Filed from Singapore for Thursday: Brent down nearly 9 percent overnight and about 20 percent on the week, testing $93.50; the dollar at a one-month low of $1.1273 per euro; the ten-year yield at 4.87 percent in early Tokyo trade; the KOSPI down 4 percent, Taiwan down 1.8 percent, the Nikkei down 0.5 percent; solar shares up the most; and the Melbourne strategist’s sentence on the magnitude of the victory catching markets off guard.

Subjective
Dow Jones Newswires, via Morningstar — oil extends decline, Asian stocks mixed

Thursday, 01:02 ET: oil extending its decline into the Asian session, front-month West Texas Intermediate down 1.4 percent at $86.93 and Brent down 0.8 percent at $93.85; Asian stocks mixed on brighter prospects for Middle East peace and a cloudier outlook for AI spending; the 10-year Japanese government bond yield down 5.8 basis points to 2.76 percent; and the president’s Wall Street Journal acknowledgment that the war contributed to the losses, without regret.

Subjective
investingLive — Asia-Pacific market news, Thursday

The later state of the Asian session: the KOSPI down about 4.8 percent after a sidecar halted program trading, the Nikkei down about 1.5 percent while the Topix rose about 1.4 percent, Shanghai up about 3.6 percent and the Hang Seng about 3 percent, SoftBank down about 5.8 percent with the report of China blocking its ABB robotics acquisition, Brent around $97 and West Texas Intermediate around $88 in its figures, gold at about $4,135, and the Revolutionary Guards’ claims of tanker fires and a mine strike in the strait, noted as unverified.

Subjective
Devdiscourse — chip stocks, oil sink in the aftermath

The Reuters markets file in a second carrying: the KOSPI down nearly 6 percent in its figures, Taiwan down over 3 percent and poised for its worst week since April 2025, European futures up 0.2 percent, Nasdaq futures down 1 percent, Brent at $94.21 testing overnight lows, and the ten-year yield at 4.85 percent in its last state.

Subjective
Outlook Business — Nifty surges as crude falls

Thursday in Mumbai: the Nifty 50 up more than 2 percent to 24,442.20 and the Sensex up more than 2 percent to 79,001.19, on Brent below $95 and expectations of diplomatic progress in the war; the report that the United States has approved a draft understanding passed to Iran through Qatari mediators, credited with pulling the war premium out of crude; and the strait’s share of world petroleum trade stated at 20 to 25 percent.

Subjective
Reuters — Indian shares set to open higher

GIFT Nifty futures at 24,295.5 on Thursday morning against a Wednesday close of 23,960.6; Brent down 1 percent to $93.50 after the previous session’s 8.7 percent slide; the Democratic win read as a rebuke to the president, with the tariff policy and the war named among the causes of the Indian market’s underperformance this year.

Subjective
Le Monde — the vice president’s post, and the party’s argument

The November 5 analysis: the vice president’s full post, with the war at its center, the four lessons, the 2024 voters who changed sides, and the enforcement change he is open to; the president’s answer at the ballroom site; Governor DeSantis’s extinction-level description; the commentator Dreher’s resignation call; Ambassador Haley’s contrary lesson; and Speaker Johnson’s decision not to seek the minority leadership.

Subjective
Reuters — Iranian officials on the vote

The parliament speaker’s “Americans said NO TO WAR” and the supreme leader’s written statement that American hostility persists regardless of party, printed with the two senior sources’ account that Tehran welcomed the result and remains on high alert against a compensating strike, the mediators’ intensified efforts, and the Hamshahri front page: “Iran’s shadow over US elections.”

Subjective
Al Jazeera — the supreme leader’s warning, and the speaker’s message

Anyone expecting a shift in American policy toward Iran is “seriously mistaken,” in the supreme leader’s written statement, with a wider response warned if attacks resume; the parliament speaker’s “NO TO WAR” endorsement and nightmare warning printed beside it; and the president’s distinction that it was the gasoline prices, not the war.

Subjective
Reuters, via i3investor — deal still out of reach, Qatar pushes

A senior Iranian official’s account: the two sides still far from a deal, mediators working hard to narrow gaps, the Qatari team returned to Doha with talks continuing, feedback expected from both capitals within 36 hours, and Tehran’s conditions required before the strait reopens.

Subjective
Daily The Destination — the Qatar-presented draft

Sources’ account that the United States approved the Qatar-presented draft memorandum, that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were briefed and approved it, that concessions cover the nuclear program and frozen assets with simultaneous announcements under discussion—and the security council secretary’s answer that the American reply to Iran’s seven conditions was not convincing.

Subjective
EuropeSays — world leaders offer mixed reactions

The leaders in sequence: Pistorius’s congratulations with Europe’s own security responsibility; Weidel on the broken non-intervention promise; Sánchez’s rejection reading; Lescure’s undeniable gains with the president’s foreign-policy authority retained; Tajani’s unchanged relations; Tusk’s welcome; Babiš’s expected but exceptionally large; Schaldemose’s cautious optimism for Ukraine; Mao Ning’s domestic matter; Peskov’s hope for diplomatic solutions; and Ryabkov’s counsel to wait.

Subjective
Reuters, via Duke FM — international politicians react

The collected statements as filed: Spain’s and Norway’s prime ministers, South Africa’s president’s new era in world relations, the European Parliament vice president’s cautious optimism, the Greek spokesman’s strong relations, Russia’s deputy foreign minister quoted by RIA, Japan’s chief cabinet secretary, France’s finance minister, and Germany’s parties from both directions.

items.title: What the Day Settled, What It Left Open
items.content_html:
The Midterm Elections — The Last Entry of the Day

Objective

What the Day Settled, What It Left Open

At 0000 the day’s work can be divided cleanly. Settled: control of both chambers of Congress, a majority of the governorships, at least nine state legislative chambers, and the closing prices of the markets. Left open: two Senate seats, two governorships, 26 House seats, and every question that begins on January 3.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 0000 ET, Thursday, November 5, 2026—the midnight that begins this date and closes the day before it. This edition completes the log of November 4 begun in Edition No. 3, the Overnight Watch, continued in Edition No. 2, the Midday Watch, and carried whole in Edition No. 4, the Evening Watch. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the midnight count differs from the evening count, the difference is stated here, in the open.

What the Day Settled

Congress is settled, and was settled before the day began. Democrats hold the Senate, 54 seats to the Republicans’ 44, with two races uncalled. The seven flipped seats stand and none flipped the other way: Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, and Maine. Senate control was called at 11:39 p.m. Tuesday on the Iowa result, per the evening accounting of where things stand, filed below. In the House, the Associated Press tracker in its latest state shows 235 seats won by Democrats and 26 more led, against 146 won and 28 led for Republicans—up from the evening state of 232 won and 29 led. Control is not in question in any count on the shelf. What the counts still argue about is arithmetic, and the cocked hat below prints it.

The governors’ majority is settled. Democrats hold 28 of the 50 governorships, a majority for the first time in 16 years, with five offices changed in party—Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Nevada, the last called during the afternoon. Two races remain open, in Alaska and Kansas, and neither can change the majority. Below Washington, the statehouse result is also settled in its direction: at least nine state legislative chambers changed hands, every one of them to the Democrats—the Pennsylvania Senate, both Wisconsin chambers, the North Carolina House, both New Hampshire chambers, the Minnesota House, which had been tied, and, by Wednesday afternoon, the Michigan House and the Texas House. The National Conference of State Legislatures’ accounting lists the same chambers, and Reuters’ state-level report records the trifectas gained in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin and the Republican trifectas broken in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas. No chamber flipped to the Republicans.

The markets’ verdict is settled because the markets are closed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,569.40 points, 3.03 percent, at 53,356.12—its strongest post-midterm performance in 44 years, per the closing accounts. The S&P 500 closed up 1.58 percent at 7,688.62 and the Nasdaq Composite up 1.44 percent at 25,736.51. Oil finished what it began at midday: Brent settled at $94.62 a barrel, down $8.98, or 8.67 percent, and West Texas Intermediate settled at $88.12, down $7.97, or 8.29 percent, per the settlement figures carried in the closing report filed below. The fear gauge settled with them: the VIX closed at 16.61, down 20.26 percent, and the ten-year Treasury yield ended the day at 4.888 percent, below 5 percent. Gold rose about 3.3 percent to about $4,070 an ounce. In the evening futures trade the verdict simply held: Dow futures up 0.14 percent, S&P 500 futures up 0.11 percent, Nasdaq futures up 0.02 percent, per the after-close report. The reasons traders gave are the same at midnight as at the close: the election ended the uncertainty, the president accepted the result, and oil fell on the expectation—an expectation, not an agreement—that the war with Iran will end sooner than it would have on Tuesday morning.

The Count That Did Not Finish

Mississippi moved during the evening, toward the challenger, and stayed uncalled. The USA Today live file, in its 8:00 p.m. ET entry, put the Democrat, Scott Colom, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, by 1,138 votes, with about 96 percent of ballots counted, on the Associated Press dashboard. The evening edition of this paper carried the wire’s table at a margin of 65 votes; the noon edition carried counts of 43 and 2,169 from other tallies. The leader has not changed in any count all day. The margin has been reported at four figures, and the desk prints the latest and the range together in the cocked hat. Mail ballots postmarked by Election Day are still arriving, affidavit ballots are still being processed, and if neither candidate clears 50 percent the seat is decided in a runoff on December 1. The account of why the two open Senate races could take days or weeks is filed below; its expert’s sentence is the honest one: the Mississippi count might take “a very long time—days and weeks.”

Alaska moved by eleven votes and by one point of precincts, and stayed uncalled. The same 8:00 p.m. entry put the Democrat, Mary Peltola, ahead of the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, by 637 votes, against 626 in the evening edition—with the Associated Press Senate file now showing 75.43 percent of precincts reporting, against 74.19 percent at evening. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holds more votes than the margin. Both leaders are below 50 percent, so the ranked-choice tabulation scheduled for November 18 stands ahead of the count, and domestic mail ballots are accepted until November 13 and overseas ballots until November 18, per the accounts filed below.

Kansas’s governorship widened on paper and stayed uncalled in fact. The Associated Press Kansas file in its latest state shows the Democrat, Cindy Holscher, at 549,974 votes and the Republican, Ty Masterson, at 542,929—a margin of 7,045 votes, with all precincts reporting—against about 5,500 in the counts carried earlier in the day. Holscher has declared victory; Masterson has not conceded and has noted that state law calls for another look at a result inside one percent. Mail ballots arriving by Friday and provisional ballots remain to be added, and a close-race audit of ten percent of precincts is required. In Alaska’s governorship, the Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, leads the first-choice count at 49 percent, per the accounts filed below, with the ranked-choice tabulation also set for November 18.

Colorado’s 4th District narrowed, toward the incumbent, and stayed uncalled. The Associated Press count in its latest state shows the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 174,963 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 171,711—a margin of 3,252 votes, with 91.82 percent of precincts reporting. At evening the same file read 169,066 to 163,993, a margin of 5,073. Boebert, in her first public comments on Wednesday evening, put her own figure on the record: “We’re about a 5,000-vote deficit right now, a little bit less than that.” About 30,000 ballots were reported outstanding in the district, concentrated in Douglas and Larimer counties. Colorado’s 3rd District is also open: the Democrat, Dwayne Romero, leads the Republican incumbent, Jeff Hurd, by more than 2,200 votes with 88 percent counted, per the Colorado live file, which signed off for the night with the congressional races still counting. Across the country, 26 House seats were still too close to call at 8:30 p.m., per the evening accounting filed below.

The President’s Answers, in His Own Order

On the cause of the defeat, the president gave two answers on the same day, and the desk prints both. In the afternoon, at the ballroom site, he called the vice president’s assessment—that the war was the reason—“largely true,” because the war “drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” and stated that he would decide the same way again. In an interview with Fox Business, reported in the account of his gasoline remarks filed below, he drew the line the other way: “I don’t think it’s the war, I think it’s the gasoline prices,” and, “The cause of the gasoline is Iran.” Asked when the war will end, he said, “whenever I want it to,” and, “We’re never going to let them have a nuclear weapon.” The price underneath both answers is a matter of record: the average price of gasoline in the United States on Wednesday was $4.12 a gallon, per AAA as reported in the same account, against $3.05 on November 4, 2025. The vice president’s sentence did not move all day: “The reason we lost is the war.” One difference opened inside that agreement by evening. Asked about the vice president’s future, the president said, per the account filed below: “You can have a lot of people running. Maybe nobody’s gonna run. Maybe he won’t run.”

On the Congress that convenes January 3, the president’s position is settled and stated. He will work with the Democrats where deals can be made, and he will veto what he will not sign: “They’ll send over things that are insane and I’ll veto them.” He has called himself “Mr. Veto” in advance of the session, and the account of his lame-duck position filed below records that he expects repeated vetoes to bring the majority to negotiate. An override requires two-thirds of both chambers, which neither party has. On impeachment he was asked directly and answered directly, in the same account: he is “not even a little bit” concerned, and, “I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that.” The incoming Speaker’s position, stated Wednesday and unchanged at midnight, is the opposite of a plan: no member of his caucus has raised impeachment with him, and the caucus is focused on affordability and accountability. A Republican senator’s prediction of impeachments and “all-out partisan war,” carried in the evening edition, stands on the record beside both. Nothing in the day resolved which of the three statements describes January.

The Incoming Majority at Midnight

The majority’s first argument is with itself, and it ran in the open all day. Its leaders state one order of business. Hakeem Jeffries: “We ran on affordability, we won decisively on affordability, and now we have a responsibility to govern on affordability,” with bipartisan common ground available where it lowers costs. Chuck Schumer pledges the same first priority and adds the second in stronger language than his colleague uses: investigations where the party believes the law was broken, court action, and, in his words, “legislative razor wire” for a president who defies the voters’ will, per the account of the two leaders’ postures filed below. The committee-level statements are blunter than either leader’s: “Subpoenas,” from the senator in line for a finance gavel; “LAWYER UP,” from the member in line for Oversight. The argument that the voters issued two mandates and the leaders are choosing one is filed below as it was made. What is settled at midnight is the program’s content—the tax law’s Medicaid and food-assistance provisions, the health-insurance subsidies, tariffs, and the war—and what is open is its order: which bill, which hearing, and which subpoena goes first, in a Congress that does not sit for sixty days.

The World at Midnight

Abroad, the day produced readings, not a verdict, and the readings do not agree. Reuters’ file of the world’s reactions, printed in full below, carries each capital in its own words. Tehran’s parliament speaker read the vote as a message—“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message”—and warned Washington against betraying it. Moscow’s deputy foreign minister, quoted by RIA, counseled waiting: “Let’s wait for the final results. The Democratic Party leadership’s approach to relations with Russia is sharply negative. There is nothing new about that.” The Kremlin spokesman expressed hope that the president would continue pursuing diplomatic solutions. France’s Jordan Bardella drew the European line: American intervention in Iran “carries very heavy consequences” for European purchasing power through oil prices, “so, yes, there is most certainly a link.” Britain’s prime minister said that with the president accepting the results, the focus can turn to ending wars and bringing down prices. On Ukraine the shelf points two ways at once: the Kyiv Independent’s headline was hopeful, and Rossiyskaya Gazeta read the same result as a blow to Ukraine. The desk prints both bearings. They are both reports of what their capitals believe, and a belief held in a capital is a fact the next sixty days will be governed by, whichever of them is right.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Mississippi: one Senate seat reported across the day at margins of 28 votes, 43 votes, 65 votes, 2,169 votes, and, in the latest evening entry, 1,138 votes—five snapshots of one unfinished count, taken by different tallies at different hours, agreeing on the leader and on nothing else. Second, the House: the Associated Press tracker alone shows 235 Democratic seats won and 26 led; the combined calls of the Associated Press, NBC News, and Decision Desk HQ, as compiled in the evening accounting, show 251 called for the Democrats and 158 for the Republicans with 26 uncalled—a difference of method, not of outcome, printed because a reader checking either file against this page will find the other number. Third, the president on the war: “largely true” in the afternoon, and “I don’t think it’s the war, I think it’s the gasoline prices” in the Fox Business interview—two formulations from the same man on the same day, with the vice president’s single sentence standing unchanged beside them. On the load-bearing facts of the day—both chambers lost and accepted, five governorships changed and a majority of them held, nine statehouse chambers changed in one direction only, the Dow up 1,569 points at the close, Brent settled at $94.62, gasoline at $4.12, and every capital reading the result through the war and the cost of living—every bearing on the shelf points to the same place. The triangle that remains is small, and it is named below.

What the Log Leaves Open

The last entry of the day closes with the open file, stated plainly. Two Senate seats, in Alaska and Mississippi, on counting schedules that run to November 18 and, in Mississippi, possibly to a runoff on December 1. Two governorships, in Alaska and Kansas, one awaiting a ranked-choice tabulation and one awaiting mail ballots and an audit. Twenty-six House seats, among them Colorado’s 3rd and 4th, counting on the clerks’ schedules. The control of the Arizona and Georgia legislatures, claimed by the Democrats and not yet called. The end of the war, which the president says will come whenever he wants it to and which no agreement has yet announced. The first business of the 120th Congress, which convenes on January 3, 2027—an affordability bill, an investigation, or a veto, in an order no one stated today. Until those counts and that Congress settle them, they stand in the log as open. The day is filed. The log turns.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-eight items.

Subjective
Associated Press — Senate, every state

The Senate file in its latest state: 33 races called, Alaska listed too early to call at 75.43 percent of precincts reporting, and Mississippi listed too early to call at 99.83 percent.

Subjective
Associated Press — House balance of power

235 House seats won by Democrats and 26 more led, against 146 won and 28 led for Republicans, in the tracker’s latest state.

Subjective
USA Today — the live file, evening entries

The running file’s 8:00 p.m. ET entry: Colom ahead in Mississippi by 1,138 votes and Peltola ahead in Alaska by 637, with final results in both states not expected for at least several days.

Subjective
USA Today — why the two Senate races could take weeks

The procedures ahead in Mississippi and Alaska set out: mail ballots still arriving under each state’s rule, Alaska’s ranked-choice tally on November 18, and an elections expert’s judgment that Mississippi might take days and weeks to resolve.

Subjective
State Capital Lobbyist — where things stand, Wednesday evening

The full evening accounting as of 8:30 p.m.: the Senate at 54 to 44 with two uncalled, 251 House seats called for Democrats and 158 for Republicans across three callers with 26 uncalled, 28 governorships held, and at least nine legislative chambers flipped, every one to the Democrats.

Subjective
Associated Press — Colorado’s 4th District

Laubacher 174,963, Boebert 171,711, with 91.82 percent of precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
Times Now World — Boebert trails in Colorado

The incumbent’s path described as an uphill battle, with about 30,000 ballots outstanding in Douglas and Larimer counties, and her Wednesday-evening statement on 9News Colorado: “We’re about a 5,000-vote deficit right now, a little bit less than that.”

Subjective
CPR News — Colorado live file, signing off

The state file’s last entry of the night: the 8th District flipped, the 4th District’s challenger ahead by about 5,400 votes with 90 percent counted in an earlier update, and the 3rd District uncalled with the Democrat ahead by more than 2,200 votes.

Subjective
Associated Press — Governor, Kansas

Holscher 549,974, Masterson 542,929, with all precincts reporting in the latest state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
The Topeka Capital-Journal — Holscher claims victory

The Democrat’s victory statement and the Republican’s answer that the result needs another examination, with mail ballots arriving by Friday, provisional ballots to be counted, and the close-race audit the margin inside one percent requires.

Subjective
Reuters — the state-government races

The takeover replicated at the state level: at least five governorships flipped, full control of state government poised in at least six more states, trifectas taken in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, and Republican trifectas broken in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas.

Subjective
National Conference of State Legislatures — the state legislative elections

The chamber-by-chamber accounting: Minnesota’s House flipped from a tie, Michigan’s House and Pennsylvania’s Senate flipped, both chambers in New Hampshire and Wisconsin flipped, the North Carolina and Texas Houses flipped, and voters in 46 states chose 6,139 legislators.

Subjective
Texas Politics — full control of more state governments

Full control taken in at least five states where power had been shared, the Texas House held by Democrats for the first time since the 2002 election, at least 28 governorships, and the judgment that this is the biggest single-election change of partisan power in state governments since 2010.

Subjective
MultiState — state legislatures, 2026 results

Seven states saw a change in legislative control as of 6:45 p.m. ET, all toward the Democrats, no chamber flipped to the Republicans, and control in Alaska, Arizona, and Georgia not yet called.

Subjective
The Market Breakdown — the close

The closing figures with the breadth of the rally: nine of the S&P 500’s eleven sectors higher, consumer discretionary up about 4.3 percent, energy down about 4.8 percent, Brent settled at $94.62, and West Texas Intermediate at $88.12.

Subjective
BigGo Finance — the Dow’s 1,569 points, with the settlements

The Dow’s largest single-day gain in about 19 months, the two causes traders named—the election’s end of uncertainty and the oil plunge on hopes for an end to the Iran war—and the settlement figures for both crude contracts at roughly two-month lows.

Subjective
Investopedia — markets news, November 4

The day’s market record in full: the Dow’s 1,569-point gain as the fifth-largest one-day points increase in its history, futures’ election-night fall and morning reversal, West Texas Intermediate at its lowest in nearly two months, gold at $4,070, and bitcoin at $80,100.

Subjective
TipRanks — futures flat after the rally

After the close: Dow futures up 0.14 percent, S&P 500 futures up 0.11 percent, Nasdaq futures up 0.02 percent; both crude contracts down 8 percent on the day and below $100; and the ten-year Treasury yield at 4.888 percent.

Subjective
OilPrice — oil falls nine percent

Brent down $8.94, 8.6 percent, at $94.66 at 1306 ET, its lowest since September 4, as traders priced an end to the Iran war after the White House tied the losses to the conflict.

Subjective
USA Today — the president on gasoline and the war

The president’s distinction stated in his own words—“I don’t think it’s the war, I think it’s the gasoline prices”—his answer that the war ends “whenever I want it to,” and the AAA average beneath the argument: $4.12 a gallon on November 4, against $3.05 a year earlier.

Subjective
CNN — the lame-duck position

The president’s stated plan for divided government: the “Mr. Veto” label he gave himself, his expectation that vetoes will bring negotiations, his warning on the campaign trail that he could be impeached again, and his answer that he is “not even a little bit” concerned about it.

Subjective
Diplomatic, Substack — the strains over the war

The afternoon at the ballroom site reported beside the vice president’s post, and the president’s answer on his vice president’s future: “You can have a lot of people running. Maybe nobody’s gonna run. Maybe he won’t run.”

Subjective
The Independent — the live file

The running file’s evening state: the president insisting he would start the Iran war again, the administration’s warning to the incoming majority about impeachment, and the vice president’s post recorded in sequence.

Subjective
New York Post — the two leaders’ postures

The Senate leader’s “legislative razor wire” and investigations-and-court pledge printed beside the House leader’s offer of bipartisan common ground on costs, his statement that no member has raised impeachment with him, and his description of voters who “can’t thrive and they can barely survive.”

Subjective
The Harbinger — two mandates, one chosen

The argument that the voters issued a mandate to legislate and a mandate to investigate, that the House leader’s affordability sentence answers only the first, and that the Senate leader ranks accountability a distant second.

Subjective
Newsmax — the majority’s balancing act

The incoming leaders’ two stated objectives—lowering the costs of health care, housing, and food, and investigating the administration—with the time and political capital the two will compete for, and the targets the committees have named.

Subjective
Reuters — the world’s reactions, in quotes

The selection as filed: Iran’s parliament speaker’s “NO TO WAR,” Russia’s deputy foreign minister counseling a wait for the final results, France’s Bardella on the Iran intervention’s cost to European purchasing power, and South Africa’s president among the respondents.

Subjective
KNKX — the world reacting

The headlines and statements collected at 6:04 p.m. ET: a blue wave and a blue tsunami in the French and British papers, a hopeful headline in Kyiv and a contrary reading in Moscow’s Rossiyskaya Gazeta, Tehran’s “Operation Midterms Hammer,” and Britain’s prime minister on ending wars and bringing down prices.

items.title: The Day Whole: The Count Holds, the Markets Close Higher, and Every Side Has Spoken
items.content_html:
The Midterm Elections — The Evening File

Objective

The Day Whole: The Count Holds, the Markets Close Higher, and Every Side Has Spoken

The day’s developments whole at 1800: the count stands where the morning left it, the Dow closes up 1,569 points, oil falls near nine percent, the president spends his afternoon at a construction site, the vice president names the war as the reason, and the incoming majority states its program and its limit.

By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Wednesday, November 4, 2026. This edition completes the day begun in Edition No. 1, the Morning Watch, continued in Edition No. 2, the Midday Watch, and in Edition No. 3, the Overnight Watch. Those editions stand unrevised, as a log stands. Where the evening count differs from the noon count, the difference is stated here, in the open.

The Count at Evening

The top of the count did not move all day, and no source on the shelf disputes it. Democrats hold the Senate and the House. The Senate stands at 54 seats for the Democrats and 44 for the Republicans, with two races uncalled, in Alaska and Mississippi. The seven flipped Senate seats stand: Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, and Maine. In the House, the Associated Press tracker in its evening state shows 232 seats called for the Democrats and 29 more led, against 138 called and 36 led for the Republicans. The noon edition carried the same tracker at 232 called and 30 led for the Democrats: one lead changed hands during the afternoon, and the called totals did not move. The final size of the House majority is the remaining arithmetic question; the projections in circulation run from 251 to 268 Democratic seats—a disagreement about uncalled western districts, not about control.

The governors’ map finished its movement. Nevada’s race, uncalled at noon, has been called for the Democrat, Aaron Ford, the fifth governorship to change parties, after Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas. The Associated Press governors’ file in its evening state lists two races still open, Alaska and Kansas. The standing tally is 28 governorships for the Democrats and 20 for the Republicans, a Democratic majority of the offices for the first time in 16 years, per the account of the governors’ races filed below. In Kansas, the Democrat, Cindy Holscher, leads the Republican, Ty Masterson, by about 5,500 votes, 50.3 percent to 49.7, in the NBC count; she has declared victory, and the margin inside one percent requires an automatic audit of ten percent of precincts under Kansas law. In Alaska, the Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, led the first-choice count Wednesday morning; the ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for November 18.

The Open Races at Evening

Alaska’s Senate race is where the noon edition left it. The Associated Press count still shows the Democrat, Mary Peltola, at 102,701 votes and the incumbent Republican, Dan Sullivan, at 102,075, a lead of 626 votes, with 74.19 percent of precincts reporting. A second candidate named Daniel Sullivan holds 3,583 votes. Newsmax’s account records the procedure ahead: absentee ballots arrive for up to 15 days, the ranked-choice tabulation follows, and the race could remain unresolved until near Thanksgiving. The Justice Department has appealed a lawsuit seeking an investigation of the result if the incumbent loses narrowly enough that the namesake candidate made the difference, per USA Today’s live file.

Mississippi’s Senate margin is still counted three ways. The Associated Press count carried at noon—462,857 votes for the Democrat, Scott Colom, against 462,792 for the incumbent Republican, Cindy Hyde-Smith, a margin of 65 votes, with 99.83 percent of precincts reporting—stands in the wire’s evening table. Other counts put the margin at 43 votes, and The Hill, citing Decision Desk HQ, reported 2,169. Neither candidate has declared victory. Mail and provisional ballots are still being processed, and if neither candidate clears 50 percent the seat is decided in a runoff on December 1.

Colorado’s 4th District moved a little, toward the challenger. The Associated Press count in its evening state shows the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, at 169,066 votes and the incumbent Republican, Lauren Boebert, at 163,993, a margin of 5,073 votes, with 83.14 percent of precincts reporting. At noon the same file read 168,729 to 163,835. The race remains too early to call. The new Congress convenes on January 3, 2027; until then the counting continues on the clerks’ schedules, not on Washington’s.

The Markets at the Close

The stock market closed higher, and by a record margin for the day after a midterm. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,569.40 points, 3.03 percent, at 53,356.12. The S&P 500 closed up 1.58 percent at 7,688.62, its best day in three months. The Nasdaq Composite closed up 1.44 percent at 25,736.51. The figures agree across the closing accounts filed below, including the closing report that records Amazon up 6 percent and the memory shares sold off, and the account that states the comparison the day will be filed under: the Dow’s strongest post-midterm performance in 44 years. The reasons traders gave did not change during the day: the election ended the uncertainty, the president accepted the results, and divided government limits the range of policy either side can enact. The exception named at noon remained the exception at the close: shares tied to data-center construction weakened.

Oil fell all afternoon, and the day’s figures do not reconcile into one price, because they were taken at different hours of a falling market. The morning file had Brent up 0.7 percent at $104.36 a barrel. The midday report carried Brent down 3.09 percent at $100.40. By early afternoon, OilPrice’s report, timed at 1306 ET, had Brent down $8.94, 8.6 percent, at $94.66, its lowest since September 4, and West Texas Intermediate down $8.01, 8.3 percent, at $88.08. The Associated Press figures carried by TT News put Brent down 9.2 percent at $94.11. The desk prints the range: Brent fell from above $104 in the morning to the neighborhood of $94 in the afternoon, about nine percent on the day, on the same reasoning in every account—that the election, and the administration’s own statements tying the loss to the war, raised the expectation of an end to the conflict in Iran. No agreement has been announced. The war continues. The price records an expectation, stated here as one.

The President in the Afternoon

The president’s first public appearance of the day was at a construction site. He visited the White House ballroom site to mark the installation of its final beam, spoke to the construction workers, and signed the beam with a marker, adding the word “Love!” USA Today’s account records his words on the project: “To me, it’s relaxing.” The New York Post’s account records that he spoke for 25 minutes about his construction projects before taking questions about the election.

His answers are the administration’s considered position at evening. Asked whether he regretted his campaign strategy, he said he did not: “No, look, if I were on the ballot we would have won.” Of Vice President Vance’s statement that the war was the reason for the loss, he said, “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” and then stated his own position in full: “But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.” Of the Congress that convenes on January 3, he predicted, “I’ll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive.” He denied speculation that he will remove the Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth. The exit polls printed with the Post’s account found 71 percent of voters saying Congress must do more to check the president and 62 percent blaming him personally for higher prices. Both records stand: the numbers, and the president’s answers to them.

The Vice President’s Accounting, and the Party’s

The fullest Republican account of the defeat came from the vice president, in a long post on X. Its central sentence is short: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.” The post states that the problem was not turnout—“Our voters showed up”—but conversion: many who voted for the Republican ticket in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. It lists the four answers those voters gave: end the war; focus on the cost of living and inflation; put America First; change the country’s relationship to Israel. To the war’s defenders: “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.” To those who warned against the conflict: “You were right, you did tell us so.” The Daily Caller’s account and the wire account carried by the Rapid City Post agree on the wording. The difference inside the administration’s own record is the day’s clearest disagreement between allies: the president called the war a piece of the result; the vice president called it the reason.

The party’s wider argument ran along the same lines, in public, all day. Fox News’ roundup collects the responses: a columnist calling the night “a catastrophic night for Republicans”; a radio host writing, “Sometimes you get your a— kicked, and deserve it”; a commentator writing that the president “launched an unpopular and pointless war. Gas prices are too high. People can’t afford groceries”; and a second host listing causes beyond the war—corruption, tariffs, deportations, the redistricting push, the ballroom. The Washington Examiner’s account records the other side: a White House official said candidate quality was the failure, and a former deputy press secretary answered that voters took the president at his word when he told them to vote as if he were on the ballot. In Texas, a Republican lobbyist told the BBC, in the account filed below: “It’s on him. It’s a total, complete rejection of President Trump.” One institutional fact belongs here: the Speaker, Mike Johnson, told his staff Wednesday morning that he will not run for minority leader, per the USA Today live file.

The Incoming Majority at Evening

The incoming majority spent the day stating its program and its order of business. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become the first Black Speaker, stated the program in one sentence: “We ran on affordability, we won decisively on affordability, and now we have a responsibility to govern on affordability.” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer pledged both halves of the mandate the party claims—lower prices, and investigations where the party believes the administration has violated the law. The Wall Street Journal’s accounting lists the items: reversal of parts of the president’s tax-and-spending law, including the Medicaid work requirements and the reductions in food assistance; revival of the expanded health-insurance subsidies; action on tariffs and on the war, in Schumer’s words on television, a focus on “gasoline and diesel by ending this damn war, a useless, stupid war, as quickly as possible”; oversight with subpoena power; and hearings on artificial intelligence. Newsmax’s account frames the difficulty the majority itself names: delivering on the cost of living while pursuing the investigations its voters also elected it to pursue.

On impeachment, the day produced two statements that do not agree, and the desk prints both. Jeffries told reporters that impeaching the president is not a priority: “I haven’t had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment,” and, “We’ve been relentlessly focused on affordability and accountability.” The first named official in the accountability file is not the president but the Secretary of War: the incoming chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, Adam Smith, has pledged to investigate Hegseth, the conduct of the Iran war, and the removal of senior military officers, per the USA Today live file, which also records a Republican senator, Thom Tillis, saying, “Pete Hegseth has a reckoning.” Senator Ted Cruz, speaking on an election-night program, predicted the opposite of Jeffries’ statement: impeachments of the president and of Cabinet members, beginning with a push against Hegseth in the lame duck, and “all-out partisan war.” The account of Cruz’s remarks is filed below. The president denied that he will remove Hegseth.

The World at Evening

By evening the foreign responses had sorted themselves into positions. Reuters’ report on the European parties that had stood closest to the president records them moving away from him during the day, naming the same cause the vice president named: the war in Iran and the cost of living. Germany’s Alice Weidel said the president had promised his voters not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy and that “this broken promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans.” Italy’s Matteo Salvini attributed the result above all to wars, international tensions, and the increase in the cost of living. Reuters’ survey of the result’s effects abroad records the Gulf governments’ reading, from two sources familiar with their thinking: the president now has more reason to seek a peace agreement, and another full-scale assault on Iran is less likely. Together the statements establish the day’s last point: the same two causes—the war and the price of living—are named in Washington by the vice president, in Paris and Berlin by the president’s former allies, and in Tehran by the parliament speaker who read the vote as a no to war. On that much, at 1800, every side agrees, and agrees on nothing else.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings never give a point; they give a small triangle, and this paper prints the triangle. First, Mississippi: one Senate seat carried at 43 votes, at 65 votes, and at 2,169 votes by three counts taken from the same unfinished tally—the leader agreed, the margin not settled. Second, oil: $104.36 in the morning, $100.40 at midday, and the neighborhood of $94 in the afternoon—not a disagreement but a descent, printed as a range because no single figure is the day’s price. Third, impeachment: the incoming Speaker says no member has raised it; a Republican senator predicts it as the first business of the new Congress; the Pentagon official both parties name is the same man. On the load-bearing facts of the day—the count unchanged at the top, Nevada completing the governors’ map, the Dow closing up 1,569 points, oil down about nine percent, the president accepting the result while stating he would fight the war again, the vice president naming the war as the reason, and the incoming majority naming affordability as its first business and investigations as its second—every bearing on the shelf points to the same place. What remains open is counted in votes in Alaska and Mississippi, in precincts in Colorado and Kansas, and in a Congress that does not sit until January 3. The evening file closes there.

The Clippings Filed With This Edition

Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-four items.

Subjective
Associated Press — House balance of power

232 House seats called for Democrats and 29 more led, against 138 called and 36 led for Republicans, in the tracker’s evening state.

Subjective
Associated Press — Governor, every state

The running governors’ file: Nevada listed as called, Alaska and Kansas listed as too early to call, and the remaining 33 races called state by state.

Subjective
Newsmax — Alaska and Mississippi, too close to call

The two open Senate races could take days or weeks to resolve; Mississippi’s mail and provisional ballot clocks and the absence of an automatic recount, and Alaska’s 15-day absentee window and ranked-choice procedure, are set out in the story.

Subjective
Associated Press — Colorado’s 4th District

Laubacher 169,066, Boebert 163,993, with 83.14 percent of precincts reporting in the evening state of the count. The race is labeled too early to call.

Subjective
North Dakota Monitor — the governors’ majority

Democrats flipped governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas and defended the competitive races in Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin, for 28 offices to the Republicans’ 20, with Alaska and Kansas uncalled.

Subjective
TradingKey — the close

At the close, the Dow up 3.03 percent at 53,356.12, the Nasdaq up 1.44 percent at 25,736.51, and the S&P 500 up 1.58 percent at 7,688.62; Amazon up 6 percent, the memory shares sold off, and the Texas result’s effect on data-center construction stated.

Subjective
The Motley Fool — the close, with the comparison

The Dow’s 3.03 percent rise is its best post-midterm performance in 44 years; the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq close higher with it, oil retreats, and Trump Media & Technology Group falls sharply on the results.

Subjective
OilPrice — oil falls nine percent

Brent down $8.94, 8.6 percent, at $94.66 at 1306 ET, its lowest since September 4, and West Texas Intermediate down $8.01 at $88.08, as traders priced an end to the Iran war after the White House tied the losses to the conflict; the inventory figures are printed with the prices.

Subjective
TT News — oil below $95

Brent down 9.2 percent at $94.11 a barrel, below $100 for the first time in nearly a month, with the markets soaring on the midterm results and the vice president’s statement on the war printed as the day’s context.

Subjective
USA Today — the president at the ballroom site

The president’s first public appearance after the results: the final beam of the ballroom, his statement that the project relaxes him, his statement of no regrets on the campaign, and his afternoon statement that the vice president’s assessment of the war was largely true and that he would decide the same way again.

Subjective
New York Post — the ballroom, the beam, the questions

Twenty-five minutes on the construction projects—the Corinthian columns, the helipad—before the questions; the signed beam; the prediction of getting along with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive; the denial of the Hegseth speculation; and the exit-poll figures printed with the story.

Subjective
USA Today — the live file, afternoon entries

The running file’s afternoon: the Pentagon chief as a possible first casualty of the result, with the incoming Armed Services chairman’s pledge and a Republican senator’s “reckoning”; Jeffries’ statement that impeachment of the president is not a priority; the Speaker’s decision not to run for minority leader; and the Justice Department’s Alaska appeal.

Subjective
Daily Caller — the vice president’s post

The vice president’s accounting in full: the war as the reason, the four answers the switching voters gave, the challenge to the war’s defenders to argue the Senate was a price worth paying, and the warning of gaslighting to come in the party’s argument.

Subjective
Rapid City Post — the vice president and the president on the war

The vice president’s post and the president’s afternoon answer printed together: “largely true” on the gasoline prices, the war worth pursuing in the president’s statement, and the reading of the post as a first step in the party’s post-election argument.

Subjective
Fox News — the stunned responses

The responses collected: “catastrophic,” a deserved defeat, the war and gas prices and groceries named as the causes, the president’s chosen candidates named as a cause, and one host’s longer list—corruption, tariffs, deportations, redistricting, the ballroom.

Subjective
Washington Examiner — the search for scapegoats

The president blaming the candidates and the war before the returns were complete, the White House official blaming candidate quality, the former deputy press secretary answering that voters voted as if the president were on the ballot, and the defiant mood inside the White House, each printed with its speaker.

Subjective
NPO Reports — the anger, with the BBC’s interviews

Republican anger at the president after the losses in Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina: “a disaster of the first magnitude,” “a total, complete rejection,” the war, the tariffs, and the immigration enforcement named as the causes, in the speakers’ own words.

Subjective
The Wall Street Journal — the new agenda

The incoming majority’s program itemized: the tax law’s Medicaid and food-assistance provisions, the health-insurance subsidies, health care and electricity and gasoline, oversight and subpoenas, artificial intelligence hearings, tariffs and the war, and Social Security’s financing.

Subjective
Newsmax — the majority’s balancing act

The incoming leaders’ two stated objectives—lowering the costs of health care, housing, and food, and investigating the administration—with Jeffries’ affordability sentence and Schumer’s pledge to pursue both, and the time and capital the two will compete for.

Subjective
Daily Caller — the first glimpse of the oversight

Members naming the officials they intend to investigate, and Jeffries’ statement at the Wednesday press conference: no member of his caucus has talked to him about impeachment, and the caucus has been relentlessly focused on affordability and accountability.

Subjective
The Rothman Report — the prediction of impeachment

A Republican senator’s election-night prediction: impeachments of the president and of Cabinet members, a push against the Secretary of War in the lame duck, a freeze on judges, and “all-out partisan war”—with the existing articles against the secretary and their authors recorded in the story.

Subjective
UNILAD — the historian’s four reasons

Four strikes against the party in power—the war in Iran, the economy and the cost of everyday life, corruption and the health of the democracy, and the president’s unpopularity as the sum of the other three—and the advice printed with them: investigations, but not impeachment, as the watchword.

Subjective
Reuters — the distancing in Europe

The European party leaders who had stood closest to the president moving away from him during the day, naming the Iran war and the cost of living; Bardella, Weidel, and Salvini each quoted, and the political advantage in the move assessed in the story.

Subjective
Reuters — the result’s effects abroad

The survey by file: Iran and Israel, the Gulf governments’ reading of a peace agreement’s chances, fuel prices, Ukraine aid, and trade with Asia, with the analysts and officials named for each judgment.
